title: Agency organization, reorganization, and competing political control
shortTitle: Agency organization, reorganization, and competing political control
summary: Administrative organization distributes practical control over policy, and reorganizing agencies ordinarily requires attention to Congress’s statutory role.
notes:
The chapter describes a varied administrative establishment containing departments, commissions, subunits, support bodies, and governmental hybrids. Congress’s power to establish offices by law and enact necessary-and-proper legislation gives it a central role in design. Early department statutes differed in their express directions to the President, and the text presents historical disagreement over how far a managerial presidency was originally assumed.

The New Deal strengthened presidential staffing and coordination, and Congress repeatedly authorized reorganization plans subject to legislative vetoes. After Chadha, the 1984 arrangement required legislation to implement proposed reorganizations, reducing the attraction of that mechanism to Presidents. The homeland-security example illustrates both a coordination rationale and the costs of combining agencies with different missions. Later unsuccessful proposals illustrate committee jurisdiction and political resistance. These examples report the textbook’s historical narrative through its stated period.

The Executive Office of the President supplies policy and management support. Special coordinating advisers can align agencies around presidential priorities, but may obscure responsibility, create appointment questions if actual governmental authority is assigned, and lack budgetary power over the bodies they coordinate. The title czar does not itself establish legal status; some such officials hold statutory Senate-confirmed offices and others serve as confidential advisers.
